title: Ninety Parallel Sinusoids with Linearly Increasing Period
lede: A. Michael Noll’s early computer-generated image: ninety parallel wave lines whose period shortens across the sheet, made to approximate Bridget Riley’s Current.
summary: Ninety black sine curves stacked in parallel, with waves that tighten from left to right. A. Michael Noll, Bell Labs era, 1964.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its print, E.34-2011 (1210 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: A computer plot built to reproduce the op effect of Riley’s wave paintings: parallel black lines on white whose period changes by steps.

context: The V&A describes a photographic print of a computer-generated image first created in 1964, and quotes Noll: “The top sinusoid was expressed mathematically and then repeated again and again. The result closely approximates the op-art painting ‘Current’ by Bridget Riley.” [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1193786/).
Riley’s *Current* (1964) is the painting reproduced on the cover of [The Responsive Eye](ref:the-responsive-eye-catalogue-1965).
observed: About ninety thin black curves run in parallel across a white sheet, in a block with a white margin.
Toward the left the curves are nearly straight; toward the right the waves become shorter and steeper.
Where the curves turn steeply at the right, the gaps between them narrow and the lines seem to shimmer.
There is no text, no tone, and no colour.
interpretation: Noll shows that the Riley effect is a rule: one curve, repeated with a fixed offset, with a period that changes linearly. This makes it the most direct reference for generating op patterns in code.
The image sits where op art meets early computer art, and that link is a natural fit for screen design.
borrow: Generate an op field from one function: repeat a sine curve with a fixed vertical offset and shorten its period across the width.
Keep a wide white margin around the line block so that the field reads as an object.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The work is by a living artist, and the V&A image is not openly licensed.
